stem: Two healthy adults participate in a renal physiology study.  Both have a serum creatinine level of 1.1 mg/dL.  Glomerular filtration rate, measured using inulin clearance, is 118 mL/min in one individual and 70 mL/min in the other.  A difference in which of the following parameters best explains these findings?​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​
explanation:
Serum creatinine is used to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).  Creatinine is a waste product generated by the spontaneous breakdown of creatine in skeletal muscle; it is released from muscle at a relatively constant rate proportional to muscle mass and is freely filtered and not appreciably reabsorbed by the kidneys.  A small amount is also secreted by the proximal tubule, so creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR.  In contrast, inulin (an exogenous polysaccharide) is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance provides a direct measurement of GFR.

In this case, inulin clearance shows that the 2 individuals have truly different GFRs despite identical serum creatinine levels.  At steady state, the kidneys excrete creatinine as fast as muscle produces it.  With the same serum creatinine level, the individual with the higher GFR filters more creatinine and therefore must be producing more.  Creatinine production depends largely on skeletal muscle mass, with a smaller contribution from diet (eg, meat, creatine supplements), so the individual with the higher GFR most likely has greater muscle mass.

Creatinine-based GFR equations incorporate age and sex to account for average differences in creatinine production, but they cannot fully account for individual differences in muscle mass.  Consequently, these equations tend to overestimate GFR in individuals with unusually low muscle mass (eg, those with amputations) and underestimate GFR in those with unusually high muscle mass (eg, bodybuilders).

(Choice A)  Alterations in basal metabolic rate can explain why individuals can have the same caloric intake but different body weights.  However, creatinine forms spontaneously from creatine at a nearly constant rate, so its production reflects the amount of muscle (ie, the size of the creatine pool) rather than the rate of metabolism.

(Choice B)  Dietary purines are metabolized to uric acid and can cause gout in predisposed individuals, but they are not converted to creatinine.  Although meat is rich in both purines and creatine, its effect on creatinine levels comes from its creatine content.

(Choice C)  Creatine (a creatinine precursor) is synthesized by the kidney and liver and is also obtained from meat.  Severe liver disease (eg, cirrhosis) can reduce creatine synthesis and lower creatinine production, but hepatic synthetic function would not differ meaningfully between healthy adults.

(Choice D)  Neither creatinine nor inulin is appreciably reabsorbed by the renal tubules, so differences in tubular reabsorption do not directly explain these findings.

Educational objective:Creatinine production is largely proportional to skeletal muscle mass, whereas serum creatinine reflects both production and renal clearance.  At the same steady-state serum creatinine level, a higher measured GFR generally indicates greater creatinine production and therefore greater skeletal muscle mass.​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​
